## Why a bakery owner cares about probability

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Ilya bakes 30 croissants a day. Unsold ones go in the bin at 20:00.

. . .

He can't know tomorrow's demand. He *can* know how often demand beats 25.

. . .

That number is what he plans with.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{python}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.6
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
demand = rng.poisson(24, 60)
plt.bar(range(1, 61), demand, color="#9bb8d6")
plt.axhline(25, color="#b4542a", lw=2)
plt.xlabel("day"); plt.ylabel("croissants wanted");
```
:::
::::

## Complement rule [Thm N.2]{.tag}

::: {.box-thm}
For any event $A$:
$$\Prob(A^c) = 1 - \Prob(A)$$
:::

. . .

Use it when "not $A$" is easier to count than $A$.

. . .

"At least one" questions are almost always "1 minus none".

## At least one defective box [Ex N.3]{.tag}

Each box is defective with probability $0.02$, independently. A shop gets 40 boxes.

. . .

$$\Prob(\text{at least one defective}) = 1 - \Prob(\text{none}) = 1 - 0.98^{40}$$

. . .

$$= 1 - 0.446 = 0.554$$

. . .

[More likely than not]{.answer}, even though each box is 98% fine.

## Your turn {.yourturn}

A website has 3 independent servers. Each is down with probability $0.05$.

What is the probability that **at least one** is up?

. . .

$1 - 0.05^3 = 0.999875$

## Two ways to count [Def N.4, Def N.5]{.tag}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.box-def}
**Permutations**: order matters
$$n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$$
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.box-def}
**Combinations**: order ignored
$$\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$$
:::
:::
::::

| Choose 3 of 10 people for… | Count |
|---|---|
| CEO, CFO, CTO | $10\cdot 9\cdot 8 = 720$ |
| a 3-person committee | $\binom{10}{3} = 120$ |
